what: AppFolio sells software that property managers use to run rental housing. One system handles listings, applications, tenant screening, leases, rent collection, maintenance requests, accounting and owner reporting.
customers: Residential property management companies, from small firms with a few hundred units to large operators with tens of thousands. The company also serves community associations and some commercial property managers.
money: Payments processing, tenant screening, insurance, maintenance contact centre and AI-assisted leasing, charged per transaction.
Monthly fee per unit under management.
moat: Property managers run their whole business inside this software, so moving means migrating years of accounting records and retraining staff. Revenue grows on its own as customers add units, and the payments business grows faster than the subscription because fees ride on rent volume.
risks: The shares trade at about 43 times earnings and 25 times free cash flow, which assumes growth continues at the current pace.
Growth is slowing in percentage terms as the base gets larger: revenue rose from $794.2M in 2024 to $950.8M in 2025.
Payments revenue depends on both the number of units and on rent levels, so a weak rental market slows two lines at once.
Yardi and Entrata are large, well-funded and attack the same customers, and RealPage competes aggressively in the enterprise tier.
US rental housing policy, including rules on screening and on fees charged to tenants, could limit some value-added revenue.
opportunities: The attached services are still early. Each new service sold into the existing customer base adds revenue without adding a customer.
Free cash flow is about $282.1M on $1.1B of revenue, a strong conversion rate for a software business of this size.
The balance sheet carries only $38.2M of debt against $107.0M of cash, so growth is self-funded.
Eight analysts average a $245.91 target, roughly 20% above the current price.
watch: Revenue per unit under management. Unit growth alone is slow; the thesis rests on AppFolio collecting more from each unit each year, so that figure shows whether the attached-services strategy is working.
